title: Safana
overview: SAFaNa (System Analytics Fauna Nusantara) is a web platform that leverages computer vision to identify endangered wildlife species from user-uploaded photos. Built in response to Indonesia's growing illegal wildlife trade crisis — where over 113,000 illegal animal listings were recorded online between 2015 and 2023 — the platform bridges the gap between public awareness and conservation action.
problem: Indonesia is home to 680 endemic species, 189 of which are now threatened with extinction. Despite the scale of the crisis, no accessible digital tool existed for the public to identify protected species in real-time or report findings directly to conservation authorities (BKSDA). The lack of this infrastructure allowed illegal wildlife trade to thrive largely undetected.
solution: A web-based detection system where users upload a photo and receive instant identification of whether the animal is a protected species — along with its conservation status, habitat data, ecological role, and the nearest BKSDA office to report the finding. An interactive map visualizes community-sourced detection data across Indonesia.
challenges: The core engineering challenge was building a custom RetinaNet object detection model from scratch — without relying on pre-built model hubs — trained on a self-annotated dataset of 11 Indonesian endangered species. Balancing model accuracy with real-time inference performance required extensive fine-tuning of the ResNet-50-FPN backbone on domain-specific wildlife imagery.
results: The platform successfully detects 11 endemic endangered species with high confidence scores, integrates real-time geolocation to surface the nearest BKSDA contact, and provides a public detection map for community-based wildlife monitoring. The project was completed within a one-month development cycle.

title: Veriface
secondaryTitle: Veriface — eKYC Real-time Identity Verification System
overview: Veriface is a real-time eKYC (electronic Know Your Customer) web platform that automates identity verification through two stages: KTP card scanning via OCR and face liveness detection via webcam. The system is designed to eliminate manual document verification, enabling instant, camera-based identity authentication directly from the browser.
problem: Manual identity verification processes are slow, error-prone, and difficult to scale — particularly for digital onboarding flows that require real-time document reading and liveness checks. No lightweight, self-hostable eKYC pipeline existed that combined KTP-specific OCR with live face verification in a single browser session.
solution: A two-step browser-based verification flow where users first point their KTP to the camera — the system auto-detects the card using YOLO, crops it, and extracts 15 data fields via PaddleOCR — then proceeds to face liveness verification via webcam. All video is streamed peer-to-peer using WebRTC, with real-time feedback pushed back via WebSocket.
challenges: The core engineering challenge was building a real-time inference pipeline that bridges WebRTC video frames (running in a separate thread) with an async FastAPI event loop — without blocking or dropping frames. This required a custom throttle mechanism (300ms interval), thread-safe coroutine scheduling via `asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe`, and a smooth lerp-based bounding box animation on the frontend canvas to handle variable YOLO inference latency.
results: The system successfully detects and crops KTP cards in real-time from live video, extracts up to 15 KTP fields with configurable confidence thresholds, and streams results back to the browser via WebSocket within milliseconds. The full ML pipeline — from auto-labeling with Grounding DINO, augmentation (10x per image), to YOLO training tracked via MLflow — was completed within a single development cycle.

title: LeafScan
secondaryTitle: LeafScan — AI-Powered Corn Leaf Disease Detection
overview: LeafScan is a mobile application that uses deep learning to automatically detect diseases on corn leaves from user-uploaded photos. Built to address the limitations of slow and inaccurate manual diagnosis in Indonesian agriculture, the app covers four conditions — Common Rust, Gray Leaf Spot, Blight, and Healthy — and delivers detection results alongside GPT-powered treatment recommendations.
problem: Corn is a critical food commodity in Indonesia, yet farmers frequently fail to identify leaf diseases early enough to prevent significant crop loss. No accessible, AI-powered mobile tool existed to help farmers and agriculture students perform fast, accurate disease diagnosis in the field without relying on manual visual inspection.
solution: Users upload or capture a photo of a corn leaf through the Flutter mobile app. The image is sent to a backend running YOLOv8 combined with Slicing Aided Hyper Inference (SAHI) — which slices the image into overlapping patches to improve detection of small lesions — and returns annotated results with disease classification, diagnostic details, and treatment recommendations generated via the OpenAI GPT API.
challenges: The core technical challenge was detecting small disease lesions — particularly Common Rust — which are difficult for standard object detection models to localize accurately. Lowering the confidence threshold increased false positives, while standard full-image inference missed small spots. Implementing SAHI significantly improved small-object recall by processing overlapping image slices with Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) to merge results, at the cost of increased inference latency.
results: SAHI implementation showed dramatic improvement in small-lesion detection — without SAHI only 1 bounding box was detected per frame, while SAHI consistently surfaced 6+ detections across Blight, Rust, and Gray Leaf Spot classes. The model achieved all-classes precision of 1.00 at confidence 0.767, with training loss steadily declining across ~150 epochs and mAP metrics converging stably. Blight detection was strongest across both precision and recall curves, while Rust remained a known weak class. The research was published as a peer-reviewed academic paper co-authored by the team at Universitas Hasanuddin.
